posts.title: Salt or tare?
posts.excerpt: Our tare has been topped up, never emptied, since 1978.
posts.content:
Every skewer can be grilled with salt or dipped in tare between turns. Salt shows off the chicken; tare caramelises over the charcoal.

The tare pot is topped up each night and never emptied. Regulars say they can taste the decades.

posts.title: How warm is warm?
posts.excerpt: Six words for sake temperatures, and the three we use most.
posts.content:
Japanese has a word for almost every five degrees of warm sake. At the counter we use three: hitohada (skin warm), nurukan (lukewarm) and atsukan (hot).

Ask for any of them; we warm the flask in a water bath behind the counter.

posts.title: The lantern by the door
posts.excerpt: When it is lit, we are open. When it is dark, we are full or closed.
posts.content:
The red paper lantern by the door is the oldest thing in the shop. It is relit with a new bulb but the same paper every winter.

In the lane, lanterns are the sign: lit means come in.

posts.title: Twelve seats
posts.excerpt: Why we never added more tables.
posts.content:
The counter seats twelve and the grill is in front of every seat. We tried a second table once and took it out again a month later.

Small means the cook can see every plate, and every guest can see the fire.
